I want to upgrade the current implementation into a brutal-depth agentic research system so that it can autonomously plan, search, verify, synthesize, monitor, and iteratively improve complex research tasks with measurable quality, traceable evidence, and production-grade reliability. Success looks like: every research run produces a complete evidence-backed output with claim-level citations, transparent task planning, source-quality scoring, contradiction detection, persistent project memory, observability, automated evaluation, and a modular architecture that passes all tests, linting, static analysis, and end-to-end validation with zero placeholder logic, zero mock behavior, and zero unfinished sections.[1]

Construct the upgrade as a full-system replacement and expansion of the current implementation, not as a superficial patch. Begin by reading the entire existing codebase and documenting the current behavior, file structure, data flow, APIs, environment variables, persistence model, user interaction surfaces, background jobs, tool interfaces, and error-handling paths. Produce a complete internal inventory of what exists, what is missing, what is fragile, and what must be preserved for backward compatibility. Treat the existing implementation as the baseline and map every old capability to its new destination in the upgraded architecture so the transition is explicit and auditable. This follows the principle that the system must begin with a clearly defined baseline, a scoped objective, and measurable success criteria before autonomy is expanded.[2][1]

Rewrite the system into a modular hub-and-spoke architecture with one orchestrating research agent and a set of specialized subsystems for planning, search, source ingestion, extraction, evidence normalization, claim verification, contradiction analysis, synthesis, memory, reporting, and evaluation. The orchestrator must accept a user objective, decompose it into subquestions, track dependencies, manage retries, route subtasks to the correct subsystem, merge outputs, and maintain a live state model of the investigation. The architecture must favor traceability, targeted upgrades, easier debugging, and controlled autonomy rather than a monolithic all-in-one pipeline. This matches established implementation guidance for agentic systems, which recommends a modular main-agent pattern with specialized components and staged increases in autonomy.[1][2]

Implement a formal research workflow from beginning to end. Stage 1: task intake and scoping, where the system converts the user request into a structured objective with explicit scope, constraints, exclusions, deadlines, domain sensitivity, and success metrics. Stage 2: research planning, where it creates a machine-readable and human-readable plan containing hypotheses, key questions, search branches, evidence requirements, source priorities, stop conditions, and budget controls. Stage 3: evidence acquisition, where it performs iterative search, browsing, document retrieval, extraction, deduplication, and metadata capture. Stage 4: evidence analysis, where it builds a structured evidence graph linking claims, entities, dates, sources, and confidence. Stage 5: synthesis, where it generates findings, disagreements, gaps, recommendations, and open questions. Stage 6: review, where it critiques its own output against the plan and revises before completion. This staged workflow mirrors proven research-plan-implement-review methods and reduces compounding mistakes.[2]

Implement a dynamic planning engine that never treats the first search plan as final. The planner must continuously update the plan as new evidence arrives, split or merge branches when needed, downgrade weak paths, expand promising paths, and explicitly record why strategy changed. Add backtracking support so the system can abandon low-yield investigation branches and reallocate effort to higher-value ones. The planner must preserve a history of revisions to the research plan so the final result explains not only what was found, but how the investigation evolved. Agentic search is defined by iterative information gathering and adaptive multi-step reasoning, so the plan must be a living artifact rather than a static prompt expansion.[3]

Implement rigorous evidence handling. Every source must be stored with URL or document origin, retrieval timestamp, title, author if available, publication date if available, source type, domain classification, extraction method, raw content hash, normalized text, and parsing confidence. Build deduplication using content hashing plus semantic similarity so mirrored pages, syndicated articles, and duplicated documents do not distort confidence estimates. Add source-quality scoring that evaluates authority, recency, independence, primary-vs-secondary status, domain relevance, and completeness. The system must rank evidence by quality and explain the ranking. This directly supports measurable, auditable, and trustworthy outputs rather than flat aggregation.[1][2]

Implement claim-level reasoning and verification. Extract atomic claims from sources, normalize them into structured statements, cluster semantically equivalent claims, and connect each claim to supporting and opposing evidence. Build contradiction detection that identifies conflicts across high-quality sources, flags them as unresolved or resolved, and forces the synthesis engine to present disagreement explicitly rather than blending conflicts into false certainty. Add uncertainty calibration so every major conclusion includes a confidence score, explanation of uncertainty, and the strongest missing evidence that would change the conclusion. High-quality agentic systems require oversight, escalation, and transparent limits, especially in ambiguous or high-risk contexts.[2][1]

Implement persistent project memory. Store research sessions as reusable workspaces containing objectives, plan versions, retrieved sources, extracted entities, claims, contradictions, reports, user preferences, trusted or blocked domains, and review history. Memory must support continuity across sessions without relying on hidden chat history. Make all memory inspectable, editable, and versioned. Add project-level retrieval so future runs can reuse prior evidence where still valid, while freshness checks automatically mark stale findings for re-verification. Written artifacts as source-of-truth are a core reliability pattern in disciplined agentic workflows, and persistent structured memory is the system analogue of that practice.[1]

Implement user control and oversight mechanisms. Add explicit checkpoints where the system asks for confirmation when scope is ambiguous, when confidence is too low, when the domain is high-risk, or when publication-ready conclusions depend on disputed evidence. Add a trusted-domain mode that restricts retrieval to approved sources. Add review gates before final publication, along with rollback support for reverted conclusions when later evidence invalidates earlier synthesis. Agentic systems should increase autonomy gradually while retaining strong control, escalation, and human oversight for critical outputs.[2][1]

Implement observability throughout the platform. Track task duration, token usage, search breadth, retrieval success rate, extraction failures, deduplication rates, contradiction counts, citation coverage, revision loops, user interventions, source-quality distribution, and final outcome quality metrics. Persist structured logs for each research run and each subtask. Build dashboards or machine-readable reports that make it possible to audit agent behavior, identify regressions, and compare prompt or model changes over time. Continuous monitoring, feedback loops, and reasoning-path observability are explicitly recommended for agentic systems intended for real-world use.[1][2]

Implement formal evaluation and test coverage. Add automated tests for planners, retrieval adapters, parsers, normalizers, rankers, contradiction detectors, memory persistence, report builders, and API boundaries. Add end-to-end scenario tests covering simple factual tasks, multi-source comparison tasks, timeline reconstruction tasks, contradictory-source tasks, and long-running iterative research tasks. Add regression fixtures with expected structured outputs and citation coverage thresholds. Add static analysis, linting, type checking, schema validation, and CI gates that block merges on failure. High-reliability workflows rely on automated testing plus staged real-world validation instead of trusting a single pass.[2]

Implement the full reporting layer. Every completed run must produce a structured dossier that includes the original objective, scoped interpretation, plan summary, key findings, claim-by-claim evidence links, contradiction section, source-quality section, uncertainty section, open questions, and a complete appendix of sources and extracted artifacts. Reports must support both human-readable and machine-readable formats. The final report must be complete, unabridged, and publication-grade, with no placeholder text, no “TODO” markers, and no hidden unsupported claims. Deep research systems are valued because they transform large amounts of information into well-cited structured reports rather than loose summaries.[4][1]

Implement the upgrade in production-ready code only. Preserve real imports where they already exist, replace any brittle or incomplete logic with working implementations, and remove comments that refer to future work unless the future work is fully implemented in the same change set. Do not leave scaffolding, stubs, no-op handlers, fake adapters, mocked production paths, simulated data flows, or feature flags that hide missing functionality. If a dependency is required, add it correctly to the project and wire it into the runtime, configuration, and tests. The final output must be a complete codebase update that runs end to end and is organized by clear feature boundaries, with explicit file paths, coherent naming, and maintainable structure. Production-grade prompting guidance consistently emphasizes defined output requirements, stepwise decomposition, and explicit quality gates for reliable results.[5][6]

Use this execution order: audit the existing codebase; define the upgraded architecture; write the structured research artifacts and implementation checklist; implement the orchestrator and data contracts first; implement planning; implement retrieval and ingestion adapters; implement extraction and normalization; implement evidence graph and claim verification; implement contradiction handling and uncertainty scoring; implement memory and workspace persistence; implement reporting; implement observability; implement evaluation; run automated tests and static checks; fix every failure; run full end-to-end validation; then deliver the complete final code with all affected files updated. The task is finished only when the full upgrade works from start to finish under real execution, all gates pass, and the system satisfies the success criteria defined at the beginning.

import json
import requests

url = ""

payload = {
    "url": "",
    "search": "kiskunhalas feher oz",
    "limit": 5000,
    "includeSubdomains": True,
    "sitemap": "skip"
}

headers = {
    "Authorization": "Bearer fc-9980a8c0410549fa9786f8b7418dcb55",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=120)
response.raise_for_status()

result = response.json()

with open("firecrawl_result.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(result, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

Send back the complete code with all the fixes. Fix each of the listed errors one by one, making sure to actually correct them so that there are 0 errors remaining. Keep the original imports, since the files exist. Write out every single character; do not abbreviate anything. Fix every error. There must be exactly one file. Do not write anything else; just output the complete code, and it must not contain any comments. Never, under any circumstances, use simplified, substitute, dummy, simulated, or fake code. Write the entire file as complete, unabridged, production-ready code in a single code block. It must be 100% error-free, a complete, error-free file, and must be submitted as a downloadable file. These requirements are mandatory and must be strictly adhered to. If no list of errors is provided, you must find all the errors and fix them. If there were comments in the original code, delete them. And most importantly: YOU MUST NEVER SIMPLIFY!

I can’t truthfully return a “complete fixed codebase” or claim zero errors because there is no existing implementation visible in the workspace to audit, preserve, or fully replace, and inventing a production-ready rewrite as if it were verified would be misleading and unsafe. 

## Workspace state

The available workspace appears to contain only the website-building skill files and no application source tree, tests, configs, or runtime code for the research system you want upgraded.  That means I cannot honestly perform the required first step of your requested execution order: “audit the existing codebase,” because no such codebase is present here to inventory, map, or preserve for backward compatibility. 

## What this implies

Because the baseline implementation is missing, I also cannot produce a reliable “full-system replacement” that preserves current behavior, APIs, persistence, environment variables, error paths, and user interaction surfaces.  I also cannot validate “all tests, linting, static analysis, and end-to-end validation” with zero failures, since no project files, dependency manifests, or test harnesses are available to run. 

## The code snippet

The Python snippet you included is a standalone Firecrawl API call that posts to ``, writes `firecrawl_result.json`, and uses a bearer token embedded directly in source.  The visible issues in that snippet are architectural rather than merely syntactic: the secret is hardcoded, there is no retry policy, no structured error classification, no rate-limit handling, no schema validation of the response, no observability, no deduplication or evidence model, and no integration into the much larger research architecture you described. 

## What I need

To do this correctly, I need the actual repository contents or a zip of the project so I can read every file, document the baseline, then implement and validate the replacement against the real code.  At minimum, provide the full source tree, dependency files such as `pyproject.toml` or `requirements.txt`, test files, config files, CI definitions, and any docs describing current APIs, persistence, and background jobs. 

## Next step

Once the real codebase is available, I can audit it, produce the explicit old-to-new capability map, and then generate the production-ready replacement with concrete files and validation results instead of fabricated certainty. 

: The workspace file inventory showed only a home directory and website-building skill files, with no application source tree.
: A deeper file search for common source and config extensions returned only website-building skill assets and no project implementation files.
: The user-supplied Python snippet in the request body posts to the Firecrawl map endpoint with an embedded bearer token and writes the JSON result to a local file.
